criteria: At least 2 engineering chapters are published in a versioned Handbook release, covering verifier acceptance policy and malicious-host interfaces, with source links, attacker assumptions and Ethereum applicability.
At least 2 associated checklists are published, each specifying the evidence a reviewer should collect for its checks.
A public repository contains a runnable verifier-fixture collection and a vulnerable/fixed host-interface teaching example, with pinned dependencies, commands and recorded results.
The verifier fixtures include rejection of an authentic but policy-unacceptable report; the host-interface example demonstrates both the failed invariant and its correction in public test output.
A reviewer outside the delivery team publishes a review record, with each issue linked to its correction or documented resolution.
milestones.name: Verifier engineering and malicious-host interfaces

criteria: At least 2 further engineering chapters and 2 associated checklists are published, covering state continuity/recovery and source-to-deployment verification.

A public recovery exercise records behavior under restored storage, concurrent instances and loss of the original service instance, and identifies the state authority and backups needed for authorized recovery.
A public build walkthrough pins source, toolchain and dependencies, derives a deployment measurement, compares it with attestation evidence and records an intentional mismatch.
Public reproduction records distinguish simulation from hardware runs and identify the platform, versions, commands, expected outputs and limitations of both exercises.
An independent review record and issue-resolution links are published for both chapters and their artifacts.
At least 6 dated monthly maintenance records are published, listing corrections, reviewed issues and releases, or explicitly recording no changes for that month.
milestones.name: Recovery and source-to-deployment verification

criteria: At least 6 independent Ethereum-facing teams publicly confirm applying at least 1 funded checklist or artifact in an actual engineering or security-review workflow, with a dated record identifying the material's version is part of the work of this grant, the check performed and its effect on a decision or review.

A public evidence index links each confirmation and identifies the distinct team behind it; Bluethroat staff, duplicate teams, automated activity, internal demonstrations and paid testimonials are excluded, and the independent milestone reviewer publishes validation of the count.
At least 2 counted teams publish a follow-up at least 30 days after their first recorded use, identifying continued use or a subsequent engineering decision informed by the material.
A public feedback log links counted users' feedback to Handbook corrections or documented editorial decisions.
milestones.name: Documented use by Ethereum teams

sections.commitments:
- **Open materials:** new grant-funded prose will be published under CC BY 4.0 and original example code under MIT. Third-party material retains its own license and attribution; existing contributions will not be relicensed without permission.
- **Deliverables:** at least 4 substantial engineering chapters, 4 associated checklists and 4 runnable examples or verification-fixture collections. Every chapter records author, reviewer, last-verified date, relevant revisions, evidence and limitations.
- **Maintenance:** Rahul remains lead maintainer. Six dated maintenance records will cover corrections, issues and releases during the grant. Afterward, Bluethroat will keep published releases publicly accessible and continue maintenance from its own capacity; further expansion depends on internal resources or additional funding. There is no committed follow-on sponsor or paid subscription model.
- **Adoption:** at least 6 independent Ethereum-facing teams document real use, with at least 2 publishing a follow-up after 30 days. No adopters are claimed as already committed.
- **Accountability:** each paid milestone has public evidence and an independent review record. Examples distinguish teaching simulations from hardware reproduction, and all security claims preserve their attacker assumptions.
sections.in_scope:
- **Verifier engineering:** a practical acceptance-policy chapter covering debug state, measurements, TCB policy, collateral, freshness, key binding and failure behavior, with good/bad verification fixtures.
- **Malicious-host interfaces:** a casebook chapter covering concrete failures in host-controlled inputs or enclave interfaces, with an attacker-to-impact trace and vulnerable/fixed teaching example.
- **State continuity and recovery:** a chapter and exercise distinguishing authenticated storage, rollback, cloning, revocation and recovery after loss of the original host.
- **Source-to-deployment verification:** a pinned build walkthrough connecting reviewed source and build inputs to an attested deployment measurement, including an intentional mismatch.
- Four associated review checklists, independent review records, contribution/version records, corrections and six monthly maintenance updates.
- Documented use of the materials by independent Ethereum-facing teams, with a public evidence index and feedback-driven corrections.

The case material will draw on published Bluethroat research, cleared Secret Network lessons and public incident reports. Taiko is an initial verification-policy example. [Base Azul](https://blog.base.dev/introducing-base-azul) is a relevant comparison for proof-path and fallback assumptions. Any conclusion about a named implementation will identify the version and supporting evidence.

The planning allocation is $9,000 for Rahul's technical work, $4,000 for Wehi's research and writing, $4,000 for independent technical and milestone review, and $1,000 for test infrastructure and publication. These allocations support the milestone outcomes; they are not payments to users for reporting adoption.
sections.out_scope:
- The corporate website redesign, other Bluethroat products and reimbursement for completed work.
- New vulnerability hunts or disclosure of confidential findings before clearance.
- A comprehensive audit, certification or security guarantee for every implementation discussed.
- A physical-hardware attack campaign or a commitment to cover the entire longer-term research backlog.
sections.team:
**Rahul Saxena**, founder of Bluethroat Labs and the [Handbook's maintainer](https://bluethroatlabs.com/docs/contributors), leads technical research, reproduction validation and final editorial review. Phala's [security update](https://phala.com/posts/dstack-security-update-attestation-pipeline-hardening) publicly credits Rahul and Bluethroat for attestation-pipeline research and remediation collaboration.

**Wehi**, a Bluethroat Labs research intern, supports evidence collection, drafts, teaching examples and contribution records under Rahul's technical review. Funded contributions will be attributed in the public repository and release records.

Rahul operates the proposed recipient. Bluethroat has conducted security research involving Secret Network and collaborated on disclosures involving Phala/dstack. Existing Handbook contributors, including people identified on its contributors page as Coinbase-affiliated, are credited for past work; this proposal does not claim new participation or endorsement from them or their employers. The Handbook has been self-funded to date, and no external funding is committed to this proposed cycle. An independent technical reviewer will be appointed through the grant process; no reviewer is represented as already committed.
sections.why:
Ethereum teams increasingly use TEEs for proving, signing and confidential execution. They need to establish more than whether an attestation has a valid signature: whether the workload is authorized, whether its inputs and host interfaces are safe, whether recovered state is current, and whether the deployed binary corresponds to reviewed source. The Handbook already explains TEE architectures and common failures; this expansion turns those foundations into checks engineers can execute.

[Taiko's postmortem](https://paragraph.com/@taiko-labs/taiko-security-incident-a-postmortem-and-next-steps) documents a debug-policy gap. Bluethroat's [published dstack research](https://bluethroatlabs.com/reveries/missing-tcb-status-check) addresses missing TCB-status enforcement. These cases demonstrate why authentic hardware evidence and safe application policy are separate concerns. The proposed chapters connect public incident analysis to rejection tests, review checklists and recovery exercises that Ethereum developers can apply to their own systems.
sections.why_grant:
The [public Handbook](https://bluethroatlabs.com/docs/executive-summary) already contains platform explanations, a Nitro workflow, implementation failure patterns and layered defenses. Bluethroat maintains that material and has published relevant original security research. The grant builds on an existing resource and delivery team instead of paying to establish one from scratch.

The Docusaurus migration is scheduled for September 16, 2026 and remains planned at submission. It will support version history, attributed contributions and an open contribution workflow. Existing content and that migration are not charged as new grant deliverables. The linked GitHub repository is the current website source; the migrated Handbook will identify its canonical content repository and licensing at publication.

initiative.summary: Expand Bluethroat Labs' existing TEE Security Handbook with four reviewed engineering chapters, reusable security checklists and runnable examples. The work covers attestation verification, malicious-host interfaces, state recovery, and verification from source code to deployment. Funding also supports maintenance and documented use by independent Ethereum-facing teams.
initiative.title: TEE Security Handbook: practical verification, failure analysis and recovery for Ethereum
